Los Angeles Review of Books: Unforgettable, Unrememberable: The Thammasat Massacre in Thailand (essay by Suchada Chakpisuth)
ABC News (Australia): Survivors of Thailand's 1976 student massacre shine light on nation's 'shadow history'

content.p: In the early hours of 6 October 1976, police and armed right-wing civilians besieged Thammasat University in Bangkok, where thousands of students and activists had gathered to protest the return of a deposed military ruler. What followed was one of the worst episodes of political violence in modern Thai history. People inside the campus and on the neighbouring Sanam Luang field were shot, beaten, hanged and burned. The military council that seized power that same evening said 46 people had died. Unofficial estimates put the real figure higher.

Nobody has been convicted for the killings. Those arrested at the university were survivors, and two amnesty laws later closed the legal door on the case. Nearly fifty years on, much of what happened remains unrecorded: many of the dead are unidentified, the roles of individual units are unknown, and the question of who ordered what is still hard to ask in public in Thailand.
content.h2: Three years after the students won
content.p: The students who filled Thammasat in 1976 belonged to a movement that had been celebrated. On 14 October 1973, an uprising of students and citizens had ended decades of military dictatorship, and the students were hailed as heroes. Tyrell Haberkorn, a scholar at the Australian National University, writes that from 1975 onward, progressive and leftist activists were increasingly intimidated, harassed, attacked and targeted for assassination.

The regional picture sharpened the fear. Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos all passed to communist governments in 1975, and for ultra-royalist Thailand the removal of the Lao royal family was especially alarming, ABC News reported. Surachart Bamrungsuk, a student leader in 1976 who now teaches political science at Chulalongkorn University, told the broadcaster how the right saw it: to stop the "fourth domino" falling in Bangkok, the student movement had to be destroyed first.

On 19 September 1976 Thanom Kittikachorn, one of the dictators ousted in 1973, came back to Thailand, saying he wanted to be ordained as a monk. Students did not believe the reason was purely religious and began to protest, according to Haberkorn. They read his return as a warning of a possible return to dictatorship.
content.h2: The hanging, the skit and the front page
content.p: Around 25 September, two labour activists, electricians who had been putting up flyers against Thanom's return, were found hanged. Haberkorn places the killing in Nakhon Pathom province; Suchada Chakpisuth, a student at the time, writes in her essay for the Los Angeles Review of Books that it happened in Nakhon Phanom. The students suspected the police were responsible, Haberkorn writes. Several thousand of them, four to five thousand in Haberkorn's account, gathered inside the university gates to keep up the protest.

The university's drama group planned a skit to condemn the killings. Suchada was a first-year member of the group. She recalls that the play started before 1 p.m. on the first day of exams for first-year students, and that someone had filled the locks of the exam rooms with lime, so many students drifted out and became the audience. In the skit two actors took turns playing a hanged man, with a rope loosely looped around the neck and make-up that made the face look beaten. To her, the play seemed a modest success. Haberkorn dates the performance to 4 October; Suchada dates it to 5 October.

On 5 October the right-wing newspaper Dao Siam reported that the skit had been a mock hanging of the crown prince and that the students wanted to destroy the monarchy, Haberkorn writes. The Lowy Institute's review of Thongchai Winichakul's book on the massacre says the report was false in a crucial way: the skit had been a protest against the killing of the two labour activists. Allegations of insulting the monarchy were explosive, and the front page was circulated by right-wing forces. Haberkorn writes that dissident students were accused of being Vietnamese, Chinese or communist, and that all three stood for being treacherously un-Thai.

That afternoon a live radio broadcast, which Suchada heard at home and which carried an announcement from the Department of Public Relations, said that Thammasat students had staged a play lynching the crown prince and called them communists bent on destroying the nation. She went straight back to the campus. Haberkorn adds that by 5 and 6 October the armed forces' radio was calling for mobilisation against the students.

Inside the campus on the evening of 5 October, Suchada found students meeting in groups in the basement of the activities building. Seniors told her to help destroy documents, mostly photocopied reports and textbooks, though a few had clearly socialist titles. They were told that members of the Krathing Daeng group and the police had blockaded the university and no one could get in or out.

Between 9 and 10 p.m. she heard sporadic gunfire that sounded like pistols, and shouting that the students were communists who had insulted the king. Through the wall behind the activities building, which abuts the National Museum, she saw men in green clothes and white helmets gathering and apparently working at the base of the wall.

Haberkorn writes that the mobilisation turned into violence shortly after 2 a.m. on 6 October. Suchada recalls a booming sound that shook her building at about dawn. Then came automatic weapons, breaking windows and seniors telling her that police were shooting from helicopters. The Manushya Foundation says Thai police used war-grade weapons, including assault rifles, grenade launchers and anti-armour rounds, against the protesting students.

The student leader Surachart told ABC News that he had been among the group sent out to negotiate with the security forces outside. They were promised a talk at the prime minister's house, but when they arrived the police told them to stay in their vehicle. The talks never took place. He spent two years in prison on treason charges. "We were so naive," he said. "We thought that the walls of the university can protect us."

Suchada recalls a hoarse voice over a megaphone: "Stop shooting! Stop shooting. We are unarmed." She ran with others through a building and into the Chao Phraya River, which she could not swim in. At a pier she saw soldiers lifting students out of the water, and says she watched people who were swimming drown after being shot. A hairdresser let her hide with ten other secondary and university students. She stayed until the afternoon, then telephoned a relative who passed on her father's instruction that she should not come home but should go to the jungle. She did, joining the Communist Party of Thailand.

ABC News describes pictures of people being burned, apparently still alive, and of bodies with wooden stakes driven through their chests. The Lowy Institute's review describes the best known image, which won a Pulitzer Prize. A man is poised to strike a hanged body with a folding chair while a crowd watches, and both the victim and the attacker have never been identified. ABC adds that a young boy among the onlookers is caught in what looks like a shriek of laughter. Surachart told ABC that his own friend was the man hanged at Sanam Luang in another photograph.
Thongchai, himself a 19-year-old student leader sheltering behind the stage, pleaded into a microphone for the shooting to stop, the Lowy review says.

Haberkorn reports that the National Administrative Reform Council, a junta led by Admiral Sangad Chaloryu, announced the same evening that it had launched a coup and removed the elected prime minister Seni Pramoj. In its report the council counted 46 killed, 180 injured and 3,059 arrested at Thammasat, with unofficial estimates higher. The Los Angeles Review of Books puts the arrests at 3,100. ABC News says the official toll is 46 but that more than twice that number is thought to have died. The Bangkok Post says the exact number is still unknown, and the Lowy review notes that some victims remain unidentified.
Haberkorn stresses that those arrested were survivors. No arrests were made for the assaults and killings of the students and activists inside the university.

The coup ended three years of civilian government. The Los Angeles Review of Books counts it as Thailand's seventh since the end of absolute monarchy in 1932 and notes that twelve years passed before halting progress toward democracy resumed. ABC News says the killings backfired on the right: many students fled to the jungle and joined the communist guerrillas; the Bangkok Post says they joined the Communist Party of Thailand in an armed fight against the government.

The courts dealt with the survivors. According to Haberkorn, eighteen students and activists who lived through the day, known as the Bangkok 18, were prosecuted for grave crimes including rebellion, lese-majeste and communist activity. Two laws then settled matters. The first, promulgated on 24 December 1976, amnestied those who had seized power on 6 October. The second, passed in September 1978 (Haberkorn's abstract gives 16 September; his body text says the legislature passed it on 15 September), dismissed the charges against the eighteen and freed them. Between the two, Prime Minister Thanin Kraivichien, a right-wing jurist installed by the junta, was himself ousted in a coup on 11 November 1977 by General Kriangsak Chamanan, who began to relax the junta's restrictions.

Neither law mentioned the massacre, the deaths of students or even that violence had occurred at Thammasat. Haberkorn argues that the urgency of protecting those behind the violence was nonetheless the unspoken purpose of both. She notes that, because investigation and prosecution were foreclosed, the exact roles of soldiers, police, Border Patrol Police, Village Scouts and ordinary citizens remain unknown. The Manushya Foundation says that in over four decades no perpetrator has been brought to justice and that history textbooks barely mention the event.

Thongchai's book, as reviewed by the Lowy Institute, says the role of the monarchy and the military remains unclear and sensitive. In Thailand, where criticism of the monarchy is criminalised, the truth is, in the book's phrase, "both suppressed and self-censored". The review also identifies a voluntary silence by survivors and perpetrators alike. Suchada's essay makes a similar point: asking pointed questions about who was behind the massacre is difficult because of the possible involvement or complicity of the monarchy and the risk of a lese-majeste accusation.

Open remembrance came slowly. Thongchai describes the 1996 events for the twentieth anniversary as important in shifting power toward the victims' memories, with exhibitions, speeches and art on the same grounds where students had been killed, but organisers removed the Dao Siam front page at the last moment, fearing a new lese-majeste controversy, according to the Lowy review. A low six-metre granite monument, inscribed with the date and with the carved faces of several of the students killed, was unveiled at Thammasat in 2000. Thongchai reads its location within the campus and its date-only inscription as memory that "speaks as much as is allowed".

In 2016, the fortieth anniversary, a group of academics and activists founded a documentation project. In 2017 it launched an online archive and released a short film, Song Phinong (Two Brothers), about the murder of the two labour activists, according to the Los Angeles Review of Books. The Bangkok Post reported on the project's work in 2017, and the Manushya Foundation points readers to the archive at doct6.com. The 2016 anniversary programme included a physical-theatre piece about the mob, Fundamental, due to be performed at Thammasat at dawn on the anniversary, ABC reported. The military government allowed memorial events to go ahead but deported a guest speaker, the teenage pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, invited to speak about his experiences of the 2014 Umbrella Movement.

On the 45th anniversary in 2021, politicians, activists and victims' families laid wreaths at the Thammasat memorial. The Bangkok Post reported that Pita Limcharoenrat of the Move Forward Party said the state's use of force and legal action against young protesters showed political differences were still not accepted. The paper noted that the exact number of victims was still unknown.
